I have tracked down the cause of some of these problems. For me it is usually caused by using RemoteTransform3D following a bone position which has a lot of motion during game play.

If "Update Scale" is _unchecked_ the Basis calculations will introduce floating point errors over time and eventually start throwing errors in Jolt.

Details:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/115665

Yea for me mine is a collision shape(BoxShape2D) attaches to a StaticBody3D. the parent is currently a mesh that does not move, but even if its attached to a node3D I get the same result. Any kind of rotation to the CollisionShape3D and I start getting this error.

@xxwassyxx It'd be great if you could create a new issue (along with a minimal repro project) for your particular case.

I should also note, since it's not spelled out here explicitly, that Godot offers `Node3D.orthonormalize()` (as well as `Transform3D.orthonormalized()` and `Basis.orthonormalized()`) to counteract the kinds of build-up of precision errors that @mikest is likely seeing.

This is talked about in the documentation as well: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/tutorials/3d/using_transforms.html#precision-errors

`Node3D.orthonormalize()` isn't mentioned there, but you can also just call that instead of doing `transform = transform.orthonormalized()`.

There's also `Node3D.set_disable_scale(true)` which will do this orthonormalization for you automatically. Unfortunately it's not exposed as a property for some reason, so you have to enable it from code.

@mihe I think that this general issue needs attention. 

Jolt, which is now the default, seems to expose the problem more often than the godot physics engine.  I haven't determined if this is because godot doesn't report drift errors as aggressively, or if it is because there's an orthonormalize somewhere in the code that is preventing drift accumulating in the godot physics that is not present in jolt.

RemoteTransform3D is the most likely place for this drift to cause problems (and I have a ticket on that), but I think a survey of other likely areas is probably warranted.

These are very difficult to debug and trace because they are subtle and usually only manifest themselves after longer runtimes and the scale changes take a while to become noticeable.

> Jolt, which is now the default, seems to expose the problem more often than the godot physics engine. I haven't determined if this is because godot doesn't report drift errors as aggressively, or if it is because there's an orthonormalize somewhere in the code that is preventing drift accumulating in the godot physics that is not present in jolt.

Godot Physics does orthonormalize the transforms of *dynamic* bodies (i.e. non-kinematic/non-static `RigidBody3D`) as seen [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/f4f0679a2d4a2b8e6da8700412b387fc1ccad951/modules/godot_physics_3d/godot_body_3d.cpp#L371), but that's not super relevant to this issue, since this error typically presents itself with bodies that you either transform yourself or child to other nodes that do, meaning kinematic or static bodies, such as `Area3D` in your case. Godot Physics does not do any sort of orthonormalization or error-checking for kinematic or static bodies. Last I checked it just lets the deformed transform through, silently resulting in borked collision checks instead, which I'm sure is responsible for other weird issue reports found here.

It would be trivial to replicate the behavior of Godot Physics by simply removing the error-reporting talked about here, but I firmly believe that will lead to more (and even weirder) issue reports than what we've been seeing from this particular error.

> RemoteTransform3D is the most likely place for this drift to cause problems (and I have a ticket on that), but I think a survey of other likely areas is probably warranted.
> 
> These are very difficult to debug and trace because they are subtle and usually only manifest themselves after longer runtimes and the scale changes take a while to become noticeable.

These kinds of transform deformations are unavoidable over time, and will happen to any `Node3D` that you transform enough times. If you then child a kinematic body (e.g. `CharacterBody3D`, `Area3D`) to such a node it will inherit those deformations, potentially triggering this error.

As mentioned above, what you should do is manually call `Node3D.orthonormalize()` (and optionally re-apply the scale) in any long-running nodes, at whatever interval you find acceptable from a performance standpoint, since it can be mildly expensive, or you just call `Node3D.set_disable_scale(true)` once to have the engine do it for you on every transformation.

Is there any reason why that wouldn't be feasible in your project?

> As mentioned above, what you should do is manually call Node3D.orthonormalize() (and optionally re-apply the scale) in any long-running nodes, at whatever interval you find acceptable from a performance standpoint, since it can be mildly expensive, or you just call Node3D.set_disable_scale(true) once to have the engine do it for you on every transformation.

Orthonormalize _is_ expensive, so I get the motivation for not wanting to litter the codebase with them, but RemoteTransform3D, by way of example, doesn't do what it says on the box. That seems like a problem. (again, covered in a different issue ticket, only mentioned here as an example.)

It would also help discovery if the `set_disable_scale` was exported and had a description that explained why one might want to use it.

> Is there any reason why that wouldn't be feasible in your project?

My personal project has this sorted (for now.)  I'm speaking more to the general case & usability. This is a very difficult behavior for people to catch in the wild. The editor won't even show you the problem because the field views during debugging don't show the full numerical precision.

Yeah, I've been wanting to make a property out of it for a while now, but I haven't gotten around to it. I'm not sure how the editor scaling gizmo would/should behave when you have such a property enabled though, or if it should apply in a tool context at all.

> My personal project has this sorted (for now.) I'm speaking more to the general case & usability. This is a very difficult behavior for people to catch in the wild. The editor won't even show you the problem because the field views during debugging don't show the full numerical precision.

I agree it's difficult to be proactive about it. The way this error-handling is done is part of the problem here as well, as we deliberately don't report (but still correct for) errors up to a certain threshold, which is hardcoded to a 1% divergence from the valid/expected scale, as seen in the default value of `p_tolerance` here:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/0304036beda5e7bd81f4f892d7fceeebfbeff8c7/modules/jolt_physics/shapes/jolt_shape_3d.h#L93

Without this high-ish threshold you very quickly run into these errors, which is good in one sense, since you're made aware of the problem faster, but practically speaking it's also very annoying, and discrepancies in the order of millimeters (assuming reasonably sized things) didn't seem that dire, so this was the compromise we ended up with.

While it might not help people find these issues proactively, there are also other things we can do on the engine side of things to lessen the severity of this when it does happen.

Forgive the brain dump, but for example:

1. Expose `set_disable_scale` as an actual property (as talked about already).
    - This seems useful even outside of this issue.
2. Allow people to disable the error-reporting through a project setting.
    - Some people have told me they don't care about this error and are fine with the engine correcting the scale to whatever. I'm still not a fan of this idea though.
3. Allow people to configure the above mentioned threshold for the error-reporting through a project setting.
    - I would guess that most people changing this would just set it to some very high value to effectively disable the error-reporting.
4. Reduce the spammy nature of this error by keeping track of which bodies have already reported it and make sure we only report it once, or at least less frequently.
    - Reporting it only once could make it seem like it was a one-off error, which it isn't really, and might also make it disappear among the rest of the logs.
    - I'm not terribly fond of the added bookkeeping that's likely necessary for this, but maybe it won't be that bad.
5. Maybe downgrade the error to a warning instead, since it's not really a "everything is on fire" type of problem, as the severity might suggest.
    - This might be a good idea regardless, but I'm not sure if it changes much.
6. Allow people to easily convert any arbitrary convex shape (either through the inspector or programmatically) into a `ConvexPolygonShape3D`.
    - `ConvexPolygonShape3D` can be scaled in every which way, so are more forgiving, but are annoying to author.
    - Since you end up essentially "triangulating" your primitive shapes, you now have to balance fidelity and performance, since rounded shapes won't be very round anymore.
    - Sort of relates to [godotengine/godot-proposals#12867](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/12867).
7. Do the conversion to `ConvexPolygonShape3D` automatically at runtime whenever invalid scale is detected.
    - This is what the Rapier extension does, from what I understand.
    - Strikes me as a potentially costly thing to do at runtime, especially when considering drift from precision errors.
    - Doing it transparently from the physics server also seems questionable, since the user might not realize it's happening, and with convex polygons having different characteristics, both in terms of behavior and performance.
    - Similar to doing this "offline", you have to decide on some reasonable fidelity for the conversion, which seems difficult to do without some sort of user input.
    - Might work as an opt-in project setting, and/or emit a warning when it happens.

Then there's the problem (unrelated to precision errors) of running into this error when just trying to scale things in the editor, in which case we don't necessarily need to emit an error at all. We just need a `PhysicsServer3D` API for querying whether the physics engine thinks the shape(s) are scaled in a valid way, which we can then use for `Node._get_configuration_warnings`. Sort of relates to #79364.

I would also like to see the actual error message improved, to include _why_ the scale is invalid for that particular shape type. I haven't looked into how difficult that might be, but I suspect it might be a challenge doing it for the body scaling specifically.

So there is some actionable stuff here. I've mostly just been waiting for a bunch of people to complain loudly enough before I try to figure out what to act on, but so far pretty much all reports of this error that I've seen have been quickly resolved with some orthonormalization and/or `set_disable_scale`, and in most cases it has seemed (at least to me) like the project was better off with being made aware of the problem, even if the error spam is frustrating.

One of the problems with the log spam is that it will eventually crash the editor and render the session unrecoverable. This generally doesn't result in lost work as it is usually preceded by a project save prior to launch, but it's not a great experience and it further hampers debugging because the debugger gets taken out when the engine stalls from the log bloat.

The log being able to grow unbounded is a different problem, but with physics tick related logs it is especially prudent to avoid as they can rapidly take out the session.

Of your suggestions, I like 1 and  4. (Also 6, but not for fixing this problem)

1. Yes :)
4. This would keep the editor from exploding. I don't think it would impact discoverability in the slightest, but that error string should explain that future errors are going to be muted! Since this error is going to happen once-per-object more code could go in here to help expose the context. Like, walking back up the scene and reporting the object in question. A mess to do from inside the physics server, but if I recall, not impossible?

Neutral:

6. I do this in my buoyancy gdextension. It's useful in its own right, but for this issue I think it should be considered masking and not a fix.

I think these will cause more problems:

2. Agreed, disabling this is probably the wrong answer. It is an error state.
3. This is just masking the problem. If they could fix it with orthonormalize by finding the call site where the problem is i'm sure they would. Doing so is very challenging though because of context loss at the time the error is logged.
5. This will still cause the log to explode and the editor to crash
7. Oof. This would a perf _killer_ and would almost certainly break a bunch of other assumptions people are making about behavior elsewhere.

Oh and...

> I've mostly just been waiting for a bunch of people to complain loudly enough before I try to figure out what to act on

I wouldn't try to tackle any of this without a maintainer pre-agreeing to the general approach and desired outcomes, but if you know one of them I'd make some time to move this forward :)

(my understanding is that you're one of the Jolt maintainers)

(Markdown will automatically sequentially number any numbered list, so your numbers aren't showing up as you wrote them. You can add a backslash before the period to prevent it from being treated as a numbered list, e.g. `1\.`)

> but that error string should explain that future errors are going to be muted!

Yeah, that's a good point. I guess that wouldn't be too bad.

My main concern is what to do about the editor side of things, since you (in my opinion) should get feedback when scaling things incorrectly there.

Then again, spamming such an error in the Output log probably isn't a great way to do such a thing anyway. The editor does also already show a node configuration warning in the scene tree when you scale most (all?) of the physics nodes in a non-uniform manner anyway (even for cases perfectly valid with Jolt), so in a sense that would justify removing this error from the editor altogether.

There might be some tool script stuff that gets left in the dark as a result though, I'm not sure.

> Since this error is going to happen once-per-object more code could go in here to help expose the context

We already do include the parent object's name when scaling individual shapes incorrectly, and the object's name is included when you scale the object itself incorrectly as well, as seen in the issue description (and your own errors). We don't walk up the entire scene tree branch though.

> Like, walking back up the scene and reporting the object in question. A mess to do from inside the physics server, but if I recall, not impossible?

Indeed a bit of a mess to do from the physics server, and impossible if you enable the `run_on_separate_thread` project setting. Adding a dependency on the `scene` module is arguably questionable (if at all doable) as well. Whatever data we can get from Godot's `Object` representation is the best we can do, I would say.

Anything more than that should ideally require shifting the responsibility of this error-checking to the scene side of things, which is where the physics server API I talked about in my previous comment would come in, I guess.

> (my understanding is that you're one of the Jolt maintainers)

Not of the physics engine itself, but of its integration in Godot, yes.

I might take a crack at reducing the spam at least, i.e. option 3. I'm sure that would be a welcome change to anyone. I also want to try including information about what type of scaling is allowed/expected. I just need to find the time somehow.

Just hit this in 4.7.1 scaling a `CapsuleShape` to (1.9, 0.25, 1.9), I wanted a flatter bubble hit detector for my hex tile. Seemed to work fine initially, but then the editor started grinding to a halt, didn't notice the errors until runtime again. I had originally tried to modify the radius/height in the MeshLibrary editor, but it didn't seem to stick, so modified via the transform matrix instead (which is a bit of a pain, but worked). Switching back to GodotPhysics3D worked like a charm.
